Translating Sumerian text to English involves interpreting the cuneiform script and understanding the context and grammar of the Sumerian language. Here is a translation of the provided text:

1. From the distant day when heaven and earth were created,
2. From the distant night when heaven and earth were created,
3. From the distant year when the fates were determined,
4. When the Danunna gods were born,
5. When Damadinana (Inanna) held the office of the en-priestess,
6. When Damadinana was shining in heaven and earth,
7. When Damadinana [...] was revealed,
8. When the gods of the mountain [...] were bound to their city,
9. The great gods, the black-headed people, the small gods, the numerous people,
10. The gods who roar like the river, whose dust is piled up,
11. The gods who moan, whose lament is set to words,
12. On that day, the ear was opened, the numerous great gods,
13. Enki, the lord of the subterranean waters, the place where the gods do not know, its interior is not bright,
14. Its place is not bright, and silver does not shine,
15. The gods of the underworld are trembling, the lament is great, they weep,
16. The man of the underworld is not bright, its place does not shine,
17. Namma, the mother who gave birth, gave birth to the great gods,
18. The underworld gods, their children, were handed over,
19. [...] they made [...]
20. [...] they did not [...]
21. The craftsmen, your creating hands [...] were cut off.

This translation is based on the interpretation of the Sumerian cuneiform script and the context of the text. The text appears to be a mythological or religious narrative, possibly related to the creation and the roles of various deities.
